about: Oldest markets and fairs, market buildings, shops and trading firms, manufacturers and industrial works of the isles (research track, 2026-10-22); each with the age claim, how secure it is, and sources with exact quotes (checked by python -m bidb.evidence --check).

entries.name: Bartholomew Fair
entries.claim: one of London's chief medieval charter fairs
entries.evidence: Henry I's charter of 1133 to Rahere's Priory of St Bartholomew is the fair's founding grant; the fair was held at Smithfield into the 19th century and no longer exists. The site is the open space of West Smithfield.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Bartholomew Fair
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: A charter for the fair was granted by King Henry I to fund the Priory of St Bartholomew in 1133

sources.title: Wikipedia: Smithfield, London
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: from the 12th century to the 19th century the area hosted Bartholomew Fair

entries.name: Smithfield Market
entries.age_text: horse and livestock market described in 1174; present market buildings 1866-68
entries.claim: one of the oldest markets in London
entries.evidence: William FitzStephen's description of London (c.1174) names the Friday horse market at Smithfield; claims of a 10th-century market rest on no cited document. The present Horace Jones market halls date from 1866-68.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Smithfield, London
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: In 1174 the site was described by William Fitzstephen as

sources.title: Wikipedia: Smithfield, London
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Work on the Central Market, inspired by Italian architecture, began in 1866 and was completed in November 1868

entries.name: Glasgow Fair
entries.location: Glasgow (held at Glasgow Green in later centuries)
entries.claim: oldest of the Scottish town fair holidays
entries.evidence: Bishop Jocelin's grant from William the Lion of c.1190 is printed in Glasgow's burgh charters; the fair survives as the city's July holiday rather than as a market.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Glasgow Fair
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The fair's earliest incarnation occurred in 1190, when Bishop Jocelin obtained permission from King William the Lion to hold the festivities

entries.name: Stourbridge Fair
entries.age_text: first held 1211 under a grant to the leper hospital; long since ended
entries.claim: at its peak the largest fair in Europe
entries.evidence: King John's grant to the leper chapel at Barnwell gives the first fair in 1211; the 'largest in Europe' claim rests on the 1589 charter's own words. The Leper Chapel and common survive; the fair does not.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Stourbridge fair
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The first such fair was held in 1211 around the Feast of the Holy Cross

sources.title: Wikipedia: Stourbridge fair
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: At its peak it was the largest fair in Europe

entries.name: Kirkby Lonsdale market
entries.age_text: market charter 1227; weekly market still held
entries.claim: one of the oldest chartered markets in the north of England
entries.evidence: The 1227 charter of Henry III for a weekly market and annual fair is the documented start; the market is still held each Thursday. QID is the town's.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Kirkby Lonsdale
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: In 1227, the town gained a market charter and the right to hold an annual fair every September

entries.name: Scarborough Fair
entries.claim: medieval trading fair of the song
entries.evidence: Henry III's charter of 1253 is quoted in full; the medieval fair lapsed long ago and the modern event is a revival.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Scarborough Fair (fair)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Scarborough Fair originated from a royal charter granted by King Henry III of England on 22 January 1253

entries.name: Nottingham Goose Fair
entries.location: Forest Recreation Ground, Nottingham (Old Market Square until 1928)
entries.claim: one of the oldest fairs in England still held
entries.evidence: Edward I's charter of 1284 is the first document; a fair was probably held earlier. It moved from the Old Market Square to the Forest Recreation Ground in 1928.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Nottingham Goose Fair
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: In 1284, a royal charter was granted by King Edward I that referred to city fairs in Nottingham

sources.title: Wikipedia: Nottingham Goose Fair
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: until it was moved to the Forest Recreation Ground in 1928

entries.name: Borough Market
entries.age_text: first recorded 1276 (by London Bridge); market's own claim 1014
entries.claim: oldest food market in London (market's own claim: since 1014)
entries.evidence: The 1014 date is the market's own, drawn from Snorri Sturluson calling Southwark a 'great market town'; the first record of a market is 1276. The site and halls are 19th-century (1851 onwards).

sources.title: Wikipedia: Borough Market
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The market itself claims to have existed since 1014

sources.title: Wikipedia: Borough Market
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: was first mentioned in 1276

entries.name: Leadenhall Market
entries.age_text: market from the 14th century; present building 1881
entries.claim: one of the oldest markets in London
entries.evidence: The market grew up at the Leaden Hall in the 14th century; the present covered market is Sir Horace Jones's building of 1881.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Leadenhall Market
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: It is one of the oldest markets in London, dating from the 14th century

sources.title: Historic England list entry 1286182: Leadenhall Market
sources.author: Historic England (via British Listed Buildings)
sources.quote: 1881, by Sir Horace Jones

entries.name: Ould Lammas Fair
entries.claim: widely considered the oldest fair in Ireland
entries.evidence: Randal MacDonnell's charter of 1606 is the first record; the 'oldest in Ireland' claim is traditional (Puck Fair's charter is 1613).

sources.title: Wikipedia: Ould Lammas Fair
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: In 1606 Randall MacDonnell obtained a charter entitling him to hold six fairs annually at Dunaneeny Castle

sources.title: Wikipedia: Ould Lammas Fair
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: It is widely considered to be the oldest fair in Ireland

entries.name: Puck Fair
entries.claim: one of Ireland's oldest fairs
entries.evidence: James I's charter of 1613 gave legal status to an existing fair; older origins are tradition only.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Puck Fair
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: can only officially be traced back as far as 1613 when King James I issued a charter granting legal status to the existing fair in Killorglin

entries.name: Old Spitalfields Market
entries.claim: market on the site since 1638
entries.evidence: Charles I's licence of 1638 is the start; the present buildings were built for Robert Homer 1885-93.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Old Spitalfields Market
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: There has been a market on the site since 1638 when King Charles I gave a licence

sources.title: Historic England list entry 1065750: Spitalfields Market
sources.author: Historic England (via British Listed Buildings)
sources.quote: Designed by George Sherrin and built between 1885 and 1893 for Robert Homer, the last private owner of the market

entries.name: Ballinasloe Horse Fair
entries.claim: Europe's oldest and largest horse fair (tradition)
entries.evidence: The fair is documented from the 18th century only, which does not support 'Europe's oldest'; it is at most Ireland's oldest surviving horse fair. Coordinates are the town.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Ballinasloe Horse Fair
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: It is Europe's oldest and largest horse fair, dating back to the 18th century

entries.name: Appleby Horse Fair
entries.claim: often said to be held under a 1685 charter of James II
entries.evidence: The 1685 charter belonged to the borough's older fair; the present horse fair began in 1775 as an unchartered rival 'New Fair' outside the borough boundary.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Appleby Horse Fair
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The fair was never chartered, but was started in order to compete with the existing chartered Appleby fair

sources.title: Wikipedia: Appleby Horse Fair
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: began in 1775 for sheep and cattle drovers and horse dealers to sell their stock

entries.claim: one of the finest and earliest surviving market crosses
entries.evidence: Dated on style; the list entry gives late 15th or early 16th century, Wikipedia c.1490.

sources.title: Historic England list entry 1269291: Market Cross

entries.name: Chichester Cross
entries.location: junction of the four main streets, Chichester, West Sussex
entries.age_text: c. 1501, given by Bishop Edward Story
entries.claim: ornate medieval market cross
entries.evidence: An inscription credits Bishop Edward Story (1477-1503); the usual date 1501 rests on that and on style.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Chichester Cross
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: this cross was built by Edward Story, Bishop of Chichester from 1477 to 1503

entries.name: Lavenham Guildhall
entries.claim: cloth-town guildhall facing the market place
entries.evidence: The hall of the Guild of Corpus Christi, one of four Lavenham guilds of the cloth town; not a market hall as such.

sources.title: Historic England list entry 1037186: The Guildhall
sources.author: Historic England (via British Listed Buildings)

entries.name: Royal Exchange
entries.claim: Britain's first specialist commercial building
entries.evidence: Gresham's exchange was opened by Elizabeth I in 1571; it burned in 1666 and 1838, and Tite's building of 1841-44 is the third on the site.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Royal Exchange, London
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors

sources.title: Wikipedia: Royal Exchange, London

entries.location: Market Square, Kinsale, County Cork (now Kinsale Regional Museum)
entries.claim: among the oldest market houses in Ireland
entries.evidence: Dated c.1600 in general accounts; the arcaded front was remodelled in the early 18th century. Coordinates approximate.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Kinsale

sources.quote: and the Market House of c. 1600

entries.name: Child & Co.
entries.age_text: goldsmith-banking business from 1664; at Fleet Street from 1673; branch closed 2022
entries.claim: oldest bank in the UK
entries.evidence: The business traces to Francis Child's goldsmith partnership of 1664. It is now only a NatWest brand, and the 1 Fleet Street branch closed in June 2022, so it no longer trades on its site.

entries.claim: oldest privately owned bank in the United Kingdom
entries.evidence: The founding date is Richard Hoare's freedom of the Goldsmiths' Company on 5 July 1672; the bank is still family-owned and still at 37 Fleet Street. Of the banks still trading independently, this is the oldest.

entries.name: Kilbeggan Distillery
entries.claim: oldest licensed distillery in Ireland
entries.evidence: A copy of the 1757 licence is shown in the distillery; Barnard in the 1880s called it the oldest in Ireland. Distilling stopped 1953-2007, so production has not been continuous.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Kilbeggan Distillery
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: a copy of the licence to distil dated from 1757 can be seen in the distillery

sources.title: Wikipedia: Kilbeggan Distillery
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: was said to be the oldest in Ireland

entries.name: Wedgwood, Etruria Hall
entries.age_text: Wedgwood founded 1 May 1759; Etruria works producing from 1769
entries.claim: Wedgwood's house at the Etruria works
entries.evidence: Josiah Wedgwood set up on his own in 1759 and built the Etruria works (demolished) from 1769; Etruria Hall, his house, survives.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Wedgwood
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: founded on 1 May 1759 by the potter and entrepreneur Josiah Wedgwood

sources.title: Wikipedia: Wedgwood
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: the Etruria Works factory was producing from 1769

sources.title: Historic England list entry 1195817: Etruria Hall
sources.author: Historic England (via British Listed Buildings)
sources.quote: The house was originally built for Josiah Wedgwood

entries.name: Cromford Mill
entries.claim: world's first water-powered cotton-spinning mill
entries.evidence: Arkwright's first mill of 1771 survives, cut down by two storeys in 1929; the list entry and the World Heritage nomination date it.

sources.title: Historic England list entry 1248010: Cromford Mill
sources.author: Historic England (via British Listed Buildings)
sources.quote: it was not until Richard Arkwright constructed a water-powered spinning mill at Cromford in 1771

sources.title: Wikipedia: Cromford Mill
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Cromford Mill is the world's first water-powered cotton spinning mill

entries.name: Waterford Crystal
entries.claim: glassmaking in Waterford since 1783
entries.evidence: The brand's 1783 refers to the Penroses' glassworks, which closed in 1851; the present business was founded in 1947, so it is not continuous.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Waterford Crystal
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The origins of crystal production in Waterford date back to 1783

sources.title: Wikipedia: Waterford Crystal
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: That firm closed in June 1851

entries.name: Old Bushmills Distillery
entries.age_text: distillery company 1784; '1608' on the label is a regional licence
entries.claim: oldest licensed distillery in the world (marketing, from 1608)
entries.evidence: The 1608 licence was a general one for the district, granted to Sir Thomas Phillips; the distillery company dates from 1784.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Old Bushmills Distillery
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The company that originally built the distillery was formed in 1784, although the date 1608 is printed on the label

entries.name: Stanley Mills (Bell Mill)
entries.claim: perhaps the finest surviving Arkwright cotton mill
entries.evidence: The HES listing dates the Bell Mill to 1786-7; the mills worked until 1989.

sources.title: HES designation LB4486: Bell Mill, Stanley Mills
sources.author: Historic Environment Scotland
sources.quote: To designs of Sir Richard Arkwright, perhaps with James Stobie, surveyor to the Duke of Atholl; millwright-work by Lowe of Nottingham, 1786-7

sources.title: HES designation LB4486: Bell Mill, Stanley Mills
sources.author: Historic Environment Scotland
sources.quote: perhaps the finest and best- preserve cotton mill with which Sir Richard Arkwright was concerned

entries.name: Ditherington Flax Mill
entries.claim: first iron-framed building in the world
entries.evidence: Built 1796-97 by Charles Bage with an iron frame; the list entry dates it and calls the spinning mill the earliest building on the site.

sources.title: Historic England list entry 1270576: Spinning Mill, Flaxmill Maltings
sources.author: Historic England (via British Listed Buildings)
sources.quote: Spinning Mill, 1796-1800 by Charles Bage

sources.title: Wikipedia: Shrewsbury Flaxmill Maltings
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: It was the first iron-framed building in the world

entries.name: Portsmouth Block Mills
entries.claim: start of mass production with all-metal machine tools
entries.evidence: Brunel and Maudslay's block-making machines were installed in 1803-05 in an existing building.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Portsmouth Block Mills
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The first set, for medium blocks, was installed in January 1803

sources.title: Wikipedia: Portsmouth Block Mills
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: They started the age of mass-production using all-metal machine tools

entries.name: John Taylor & Co bell foundry
entries.age_text: Taylor family from 1784; Loughborough foundry 1839, present site 1859
entries.claim: world's largest working bell foundry; origins claimed in the 14th century
entries.evidence: The 14th-century descent is the firm's; the Taylor family's founding is 1784 and the Loughborough works dates from 1859.

sources.title: Wikipedia: John Taylor & Co
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The Taylor family became involved in 1784 with Robert Taylor

sources.title: Wikipedia: John Taylor & Co
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: moving to the current site in 1859

entries.name: Belleek Pottery
entries.claim: Ireland's oldest working pottery (often said)
entries.evidence: The building was begun in 1858 and Parian ware made from 1863; the present company dates from 1884. Often called Ireland's oldest pottery, a claim not checked.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Belleek Pottery
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Preparation of the site and building began in 1858

entries.name: Sele Mill (site of England's first paper mill)
entries.claim: first paper mill in England
entries.evidence: John Tate made paper here in the 1490s; the present mill building is later and is now flats.

sources.title: Wikipedia: John Tate (papermaker)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Paper was produced there in the 1490s, and possibly earlier

sources.title: Wikipedia: Sele Mill
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: As far as is known, Sele was the first paper mill in England

entries.name: Portsmouth dry docks
entries.age_text: first dry dock 1495 (lost); Great Stone Dock (No. 5) begun 1691, rebuilt 1769
entries.claim: first recorded dry dock in the world (1495); 'oldest surviving' claim
entries.evidence: Henry VII's dock of 1495 was filled with rubble a century later, so the 'oldest surviving dry dock' claim for 1495 is wrong; the oldest dock in use is Dummer's Great Stone Dock (No. 5) of 1691 onwards, rebuilt 1769.

sources.title: Wikipedia: HMNB Portsmouth
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The first recorded dry dock in the world was built in Portsmouth by Henry VII in 1495

sources.title: Wikipedia: HMNB Portsmouth
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: a hundred years later it is described as being filled with rubble

sources.title: Wikipedia: HMNB Portsmouth
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Extensively rebuilt in 1769, the Great Stone Dock is now known as No.5 dock

entries.name: Old Furnace, Coalbrookdale
entries.claim: where iron was first smelted with coke (1709)
entries.evidence: The list entry dates the base to 1638 (cast on the beams) and the coke smelting to 1709; the upper structure is Abraham Darby III's rebuilding of 1777.

sources.title: Historic England list entry 1054135: The Old Furnace
sources.author: Historic England (via British Listed Buildings)
sources.quote: part of the first furnace of 1638 in which, in 1709 the first iron ever to be made with coke was smelted

entries.name: Catcliffe Glass Cone
entries.claim: oldest surviving glass cone in Western Europe
entries.evidence: Built about 1740 for William Fenney; the date is in the list entry.

sources.title: Historic England list entry 1132732: The Glassworks Cone
sources.author: Historic England (via British Listed Buildings)
sources.quote: Glass cone. c1740 for William Fenney

sources.title: Wikipedia: Catcliffe Glass Cone
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: It is the oldest surviving structure of its type in Western Europe

entries.name: Bonawe Iron Furnace
entries.claim: most complete charcoal-fired ironworks in Britain
entries.evidence: Built in 1753 by the Newland Company of Cumbria and in use until 1876; the HES schedule calls it the most complete early iron works in Scotland.

sources.title: HES designation SM90037: Bonawe, Iron Furnace

sources.title: HES designation SM90037: Bonawe, Iron Furnace
sources.author: Historic Environment Scotland
sources.quote: the most complete and well-preserved early industrial iron works in Scotland

entries.name: Dyfi Furnace
entries.claim: restored charcoal-fired blast furnace
entries.evidence: Built around 1755 and out of use by 1810.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Dyfi Furnace
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The furnace built around 1755 was only used for about fifty years to smelt iron ore

entries.evidence: Built 1785-91 (Wikipedia gives 1790 for completion); rope is still made there.

entries.name: Ballincollig Royal Gunpowder Mills
entries.claim: once the largest gunpowder mills in Ireland
entries.evidence: Opened in 1794 as a private works and later taken over by the government; closed 1903, now a park with surviving mill buildings.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Ballincollig Royal Gunpowder Mills
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: the powder mills were originally opened in 1794 as a private enterprise

entries.name: Northern Glass Cone, Alloa
entries.wikipedia_title: Northern Glass Cone, Alloa Glass Works
entries.claim: only glass cone surviving in Scotland
entries.evidence: One of the cones built by 1825; one of four surviving in the UK.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Northern Glass Cone, Alloa Glass Works

entries.name: Gasholder No. 2, Fulham
entries.claim: oldest surviving gasholder in the world
entries.evidence: Built 1829-30 for the Imperial Gas Light Company; Historic England calls it by far the oldest surviving gasholder.

sources.author: Historic England (via British Listed Buildings)

entries.location: Hempton Road, Fakenham, Norfolk (Museum of Gas and Local History)
entries.claim: only complete non-operational town gasworks in England
entries.evidence: Built 1846; the scheduled monument entry could not be read by script, so the date rests on secondary accounts.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Gasworks

entries.name: Lion Salt Works
entries.claim: last open-pan salt works in the UK
entries.evidence: Built 1894 and worked until 1986; not old, but the last of its kind.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Lion Salt Works
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The Lion Salt Works is the UK's last remaining open pan salt works
